extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in 19th‑century fairs, menageries, and popular entertainments (historians, antiquarians, general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive, contemporaneous account of shows, performances, menageries, and exhibition practices at 19th‑century fairs, including bills, staging, animal care, and visitor experience. Emphasis on spectacle, advertising, and conditions for animals and performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of advertising / truthfulness of bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising and show-bills frequently proclaimed spectacular phenomena (e.g., 'The Conquering Lion', 'the only lion and tigress in one den'), but such announcements were not always borne out in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether advertised attractions actually exist or are exaggerated: example—Atkins's bill announced 'a remarkably fine tigress in the same den with a noble British lion' and other marvels, yet Hone notes the promised conjunction was 'not to be seen in reality.' Consider whether claims of 'only one in England' or 'wonderful phenomenon' are substantiated by the exhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation and cage size (animal housing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper ventilation and sufficiently large cages are essential for the health and longevity of captive mammals; inadequate ventilation and cramped cages contributed to high mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts old, long narrow, artificially heated carnivora-houses with later larger cages admitting 'pure external air,' noting mortality decreased after improving ventilation. Assess exhibitions for cage dimensions, ability to admit fresh air, and avoidance of cramped, poorly ventilated enclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excessive artificial heating; prioritize ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive heating of tropical animals' enclosures was initially overvalued, while ventilation was undervalued; warming without ventilation produced stifling, unhealthy conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states: 'Too much importance was at first attached to warming the cages ... and too little to ventilating them.' Evaluate whether keepers rely on heat rather than fresh air and whether that practice correlates with poor animal condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness and visible condition of animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean surroundings and well-fed, alert animals indicate good husbandry and care; such condition enhances the exhibition's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hone praises Wombwell's menagerie as 'thoroughly clean' and notes the animals' condition 'told that they were well taken care of.' Use observable cleanliness and body condition as markers of care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, rarity, and variety of species as attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: A diverse collection and the presence of rare or unique specimens (e.g., 'only one in England', 'the only two alive in the three kingdoms') are major draws for visitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess shows on the basis of diversity and rarity (zebras, pelicans, aurochos, unique pelicans/emus). Promotional emphasis on unique specimens is used to attract crowds; verify uniqueness where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic provisioning and feeding requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeding large carnivora and other animals is costly and operationally significant: e.g., 'the amount of animal food required ... about four hundredweight daily' and a full-grown lion or tiger consumes about twelve pounds of meat per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the financial/operational sustainability of a menagerie by estimating daily food requirements and costs; recognize that feeding regimen decisions (e.g., bears only fed meat in winter) affect condition and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of training and animal docility/intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Trained behaviours and demonstrations of animals' responsiveness to keepers (elephant taking money, unbolting doors, lions and tigresses performing hoops and sitting with keepers) serve both as entertainment and evidence of proper training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality of exhibition by the elegance and reliability of trained acts: the elephant that 'took a sixpence ... placed it in a box ... bolted and unbolt a door' and the lion/tigress that performed hoops and lay quiescent with the keeper are cited as marks of intelligent, well-trained animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft and visual presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of painted scenery, show-cloths, gas lighting, costumes, and scene changes contributes significantly to the effectiveness of a theatrical exhibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include multi-scene theatrical productions with rapidly changing scenery, the use of gas lighting (a 'distinction' in some shows), and flamboyant costumes (e.g., Faustus's red Spanish mantle). Judge exhibitions by their scenic inventiveness, lighting, and costume design as components of spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer skill, novelty, and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical skill (tight-rope dancing, balancing acts, 'learned' horses, tumbling, conjuring) and novel feats (balancing swords and plates, boy dancing hornpipe on rope) are principal criteria for evaluating entertainments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account highlights dexterous feats and the quality of execution (e.g., riding and leaping over garters, balancing chairs and swords). Consider musical accompaniment, clowning, and choreography that enliven performances when assessing quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, crowd control, and disorder management
rubrics_metrics.description: Large crowds and spectacle can produce confusion and disorder; incidents (drunken intruders, lion-baitings) reveal safety risks and the need for effective management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative records a drunken intruder causing a scene in the ring and notes the 'confusion and disorder which prevailed' at crowded exhibitions. Evaluate arrangements for audience control, performer safety, and whether the management can handle disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and conditions of human exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: Human curiosities and performers should appear well-treated, comfortable, and reasonably provided for; visible contentment and opportunity for exercise are markers of humane treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Hone examined people displayed (e.g., 'Miss Hipson, the Middlesex Wonder'), he notes 'an appearance of ease and good condition' and that they described themselves as 'very comfortable' and 'well treated' with exercise routines. Use such testimony and observation to judge exhibitors' treatment of human participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical rhetoric and spectacle as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant language, pictorial representation, and processional elements are deliberately used to create expectation and atmosphere; the effectiveness of this rhetoric is part of the exhibition's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show-cloths emblazoned with names and dramatic paintings, band parades, and loud proclamations ('Walk up!--walk up!') are cited repeatedly. Assess how visual rhetoric and parade elements set audience expectations and whether they match the on-stage performance.
